lines.text: First lines. The episode opens at night with people on a balcony, including Minister James George "Jim" Hacker and the Mayor, who is announcing the results

lines.speaker: Mayor
lines.text: David Lloyd Evans, 4,106...

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: And here at Birmingham East, the Returning Officer is just declaring the result.

lines.speaker: Mayor
lines.text: ...James George Hacker: 21,793! Arthur William Gaunt: 19,321!

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: So Jim Hacker's back with an increased majority, and after many years as a Shadow Minister, seems almost certain to get a post in the new Government.
Hacker is in his new office with Principal Private Secretary Bernard Woolley

lines.speaker: Bernard
lines.text: A sherry Minister?

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Jim.

lines.speaker: Bernard
lines.text: Oh, gin.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: No, no, Jim, Jim. Call me Jim.

lines.speaker: Bernard
lines.text: Oh. Oh, well I think it was all the same to you. I would prefer to call you Minister, Minister.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Minister, Minister? Oh quite, quite. I see what you mean. Does that mean I have to call you Private Secretary, Private Secretary?

lines.speaker: Bernard
lines.text: No, do call me Bernard.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Thank you, Bernard. (Bernard gives him a glass)

lines.speaker: Bernard
lines.text: You're most welcome, Minister.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Cheers, Bernard.

lines.speaker: Bernard
lines.text: Your health, Minister.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Well what now?
Sir Humphrey Appleby enters the office

lines.speaker: Bernard
lines.text: Ah, Minister, allow me to present Sir Humphrey Appleby, Permanent Under Secretary of State and Head of the D.A.A..

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Hello, Sir Humphrey.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Hello, and welcome. (Shakes hands with Minister Hacker)

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Thank you, Sir Humphrey.

lines.speaker: Bernard
lines.text: I believe you know each other.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Yes, we did cross swords when the minister gave me a grilling over the estimates in the Public Accounts Committee.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: I wouldn't say that.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: You came up with all the questions I hoped nobody would ask.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Opposition's about asking awkward questions.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: And Government is about not answering them.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Well, you answered all mine anyway.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: I'm glad you thought so, Minister. (Bernard gives him a glass) And Good luck.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Now who else is in this department?

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Well briefly, sir, I am the Permanent Under Secretary of State, known as the Permanent Secretary. Woolley here is your Principal Private Secretary. I, too, have a Principal Private Secretary, and he is the Principal Private Secretary to the Permanent Secretary. Directly responsible to me are ten Deputy Secretaries, 87 Under Secretaries and 219 Assistant Secretaries. Directly responsible to the Principal Private Secretaries are plain Private Secretaries, and the Prime Minister will be appointing two Parliamentary Under-Secretaries and you will be appointing your own Parliamentary Private Secretary.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Can they all type?

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: None of us can type, Minister. Mrs Mackay types: she's the secretary.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Pity, we could have opened an agency.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Very droll, Minister.

lines.speaker: Bernard
lines.text: Very, very amusing, sir.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: I suppose they all say that, do they?

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Certainly not, Minister. Not quite all...

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Right, now then, to business. Now you'll have to forgive me if I'm a bit blunt, but that's the sort of chap I am. Frankly, this depart... (Sits on a brown leather swivel chair) Don't care for this chair very much.

lines.speaker: Bernard
lines.text: We can change it, Minister.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Can you?

lines.speaker: Bernard
lines.text: We can change anything, Minister. The furniture, decor, office routine - Your wish is our command.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: In that case, I'd like a new chair. I hate swivel chairs.

lines.speaker: Bernard
lines.text: It used to be said there were two kinds of chairs to go with two kinds of Minister: one sort folds up instantly; the other sort goes round and round in circles.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Now then, gentlemen, frankly this Department has got to cut a great swathe through all this stuffy Whitehall bureaucracy. We want a new broom. We're going to throw open the windows, let in a bit of fresh air, cut through all the red tape, streamline this creaking old bureaucratic machine.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: You mean a clean sweep, Minister?

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: That's it. A clean sweep. Far too many people just sitting behind desks. (Admires his desk) Not like us, of course. But we've got to get rid of all those people just making work for each other.

lines.speaker: Bernard
lines.text: Get rid of them?

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: I think you mean "Redeploy them", Minister.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Yes. Good Lord no, I don't mean put them out of work. No, no. Open Government, that's what my party believes in, that was the main plank of our manifesto. Taking the nation into our confidence. Now how does that strike you? Do sit down.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: May I? In fact, just as you said in the House on May 2nd last year, and again on November 23rd, and in your Observer article and in your Daily Mail interview, and as your manifesto made clear.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: You know about that?

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: I'd like to have a look at these proposals, Minister. They outline the ways in which this policy could be implemented, and contain draft proposals for a white paper for your approval. We thought the white paper might be called "Open Government".

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: You mean it's all been...

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: It's all been taken care of, Minister.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Who did all this?

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: The creaking old bureaucratic machine. No, quite seriously. We are fully seized of the need for reform and we have taken it on board.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Must say, I'm rather surprised. I expected to have to fight you all way along the line with this.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: People do have funny ideas about the Civil Service. We're just here to help you formulate and implement your policies.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: (Reading the piece of paper) "Proposals for shortening approval procedures in planning appeals"?

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Hansard Volume 497, page 1102, Column B. Quote "Mr. Hacker: Is the Minister aware that planning procedures make building a bungalow in the 20th century slower than building a cathedral in the 12th century? Opposition laughter and Government cries of shame".

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Well they didn't actually cry shame.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Quite so, Minister.

lines.speaker: Bernard
lines.text: But surely the citizens of a democracy have a right to know.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: No. They have a right to be ignorant. Knowledge only means complicity in guilt; ignorance has a certain dignity.
There are two official replies to the Minister's correspondence.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: What's the difference?

lines.speaker: Bernard
lines.text: Well, "under consideration" means "we've lost the file"; "under active consideration" means "we're trying to find it".
The President of Buranda plans a speech urging the Scots and Irish to fight against "British colonialism".

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Humphrey, do you think it is a good idea to issue a statement?

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Well, Minister, in practical terms we have the usual six options. One: do nothing. Two: issue a statement deploring the speech. Three: lodge an official protest. Four: cut off aid. Five: break off diplomatic relations. And six: declare war.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Which should be it?

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Well, if we do nothing, that means we implicitly agree with the speech. If we issue a statement, we'll just look foolish. If we lodge a protest, it'll be ignored. We can't cut off aid, because we don't give them any. If we break off diplomatic relations, then we can't negotiate the oil rig contracts. And if we declare war, it might just look as though we were over-reacting.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Bernard, this government is here to govern, not merely preside like our predecessors did. When a country is going downhill, it is time for someone to get into the driving seat, and put his foot on the accelerator.

lines.speaker: Bernard
lines.text: I think you mean the brake.
Frank Weisel is quoting an article in the Express about the fact that Inland Revenue has more employees than the Royal Navy.

lines.speaker: Frank Weisel
lines.text: "Perhaps the government thinks that a tax is the best form of defence."

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: How many people do we have in this department?

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Ummm... well, we're very small...

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Two, maybe three thousand?

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: About twenty-three thousand to be precise.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: TWENTY-THREE THOUSAND! In the department of administrative affairs, twenty-three thousand administrators just to administer the other administrators! We need to do a time-and-motion study, see who we can get rid of.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Ah, well, we did one of those last year.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: And what were the results?

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: It turned out that we needed another five hundred people.
There is a government building with a reinforced concrete basement in case of a nuclear war.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: There has to be somewhere to carry on government, even if everything else stops.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Why?

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Well, government doesn't stop just because the country's been destroyed! I mean, annihilation’s bad enough without anarchy to make things even worse!

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: You mean you'd have a lot of rebellious cinders.
The Minister is already double-booked when his wife reminds him of another prior engagement.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: [on the phone] Bernard? Yes, it's me. Look, I'm going to have to cancel tomorrow. Swansea and Newcastle. Well, you see, it's my wife's wedding anniversary tomorrow.

lines.speaker: Annie
lines.text: It's yours, too!

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: And mine, too, actually. Yes, it is...What do you mean, "coincidence"? Don't be silly, Bernard!
It is 2 a.m, and Hacker has just made a phone call to a sleepy Sir Humphrey.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: [hangs up] Oh, damn! I meant to tell him to come and see me about it before Cabinet.

lines.speaker: Annie
lines.text: Don't ring him now!

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: No, perhaps you're right. It is a bit late.

lines.speaker: Annie
lines.text: Give him another ten minutes.

episodes.title: The Writing on the Wall
episodes.titleFull: Episode Five: The Writing on the Wall

lines.text: One day, Mr. Hacker is taking some paperwork out of his red box and Sir Humphrey has come to see him

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: I am still not happy with this report, Humphrey.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Then, Minister, we shall be happy to redraft it for you.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: You've redrafted it three times already.

lines.speaker: Bernard
lines.text: That's not absolutely correct, Minister.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Yes, it is, Bernard, I can count. This is the third draft report.

lines.speaker: Bernard
lines.text: It's quite so, Minister, therefore it's been drafted once and subsequently redrafted twice.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Don't quibble, Bernard.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: But we shall be happy to redraft it a third time.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: And a fourth and a fifth and a sixth, no doubt. And it still won't say what I want it to say, it'll say what you want it to say, and I want it to say what I want it to say.

lines.speaker: Bernard
lines.text: What do you want it to say, Minister?

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: We want it to say what you want it to say.

lines.speaker: Bernard
lines.text: I'm sure the parliament doesn't want you to say anything you don't want to say.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Stop wittering, Bernard! Six weeks ago, the Think Tank asked us for our evidence on Civil Service overmanning. Three times, I have briefed a group of civil servants in words of one syllable and each time, they've sent back a totally unintelligible report, saying the exact opposite of what I asked them to say.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: With respect, Minister, how do you know it says the opposite if it's totally unintelligible?

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: All I am saying is that the Civil Service is grossly overmanned and must be slimmed down.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Quite so. That is what the report says.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: No, it doesn't.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Yes, it does, Minister.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: It - it does... Look, what I'm talking about is a phased reduction in the Civil Service of about 200,000 people. Are you going to put that in this report or not?

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Well, Minister, perhaps if you were to take that draft home with you this weekend and study it, you might find that it does, in fact, say what you want it to say.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: And if it doesn't?

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Then I can only suggest that we redraft it.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Humphrey? Humphrey, sit down. (Humphrey sits in the chair opposite Hacker) Will you give me a straight answer to a straight question?

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Oh, well, Minister, as long as you are not asking me to resort to crude generalisations and vulgar oversimplifications, such as a simple yes or no. I shall do my utmost to oblige.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Is that "yes"?

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: (Takes a deep breath) Yes.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Right. Well, here's the straight question.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Oh, I thought that was it.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: When you give your evidence to the Think Tank, are you going to support my view that the Civil Service is overmanned and feather-bedded, or not? Yes or no? Straight answer.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Well, Minister, if you ask me for a straight answer, then I shall say that, as far as we can see, looking at it by and large, taking one time with another in terms of the average of departments, then in the final analysis it is probably true to say, that at the end of the day, in general terms, you would probably find that, not to put too fine a point on it, there probably wasn't very much in it one way or the other. As far as one can see, at this stage.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Is that "yes" or "no"?

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Yes and no.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Suppose you weren't asked for a straight answer?

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Well then I should play for time, Minister.
Sir Humphrey stands up to Minister Hacker

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: One more thing, Minister. The evidence to the Central Policy Review Staff.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: You mean the Think Tank?

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Yes, Minister.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: What about it?

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Have you redrafted the redraft of your draft?

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: You don't want it yet, do you?

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Yes.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Why?

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: So that we can redraft it.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Well that won't be necessary, Humphrey.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: I think it will, Minister.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Humphrey, Drafting is not a Civil Service monopoly, you know.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: No, it's a highly specialised skill which few outside the Service can master.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Nonsense. Drafts is easy. It's a game anyone can play.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Not without getting huffed. So could I have the draft proposal, please?

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Certainly, Humphrey.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: When, Minister?

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Later, Humphrey.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Yes, but when?

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Well, you're always saying we mustn't rush things, aren't you?

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Minister, I must ask you for a straight answer. On what day? Tomorrow? Monday? Tuesday?

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: In due course, Humphrey. At the appropriate juncture. In the fullness of time. When the moment is ripe. When the necessary procedures have been completed. Nothing precipitate, of course.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Minister, this is getting urgent.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Urgent, Humphrey? What a lot of new words we're learning!

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Now, Minister, you'll forgive me if I say this, but I'm beginning to suspect that you are concealing something from me.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Surely you and I have no secrets from each other, have we, Humphrey?

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: I'm sorry, Minister, but sometimes one is forced to consider the possibility that affairs are being conducted in a way which, all things being considered, and making all possible allowances, is, not to put too fine a point on it, perhaps not entirely straightforward.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Well you're the expert on straightforwardness.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: So what about the draft evidence to the Central Policy Review Staff?

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Well, since you ask, Humphrey, and to be perfectly straightforward, I have redrafted it myself. I don't want you to redraft it. (Gets out of his seat and picks up his red box which he will put the redraft in) I am perfectly happy with it as it is. (Walks over to the fireplace)

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: May I be bold enough to ask what you have said?

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: I've said what I wanted to say: Phased reductions in the Civil Service.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Yes, but I...

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Humphrey, you have frustrated me over open government, you have frustrated me over the economy drive, but this time I'm going to have my way. The party wants it, the public wants it. And I'm bound to say that all we get from the Civil Service is delaying tactics.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Well, I wouldn't call Civil Service delays "tactics", Minister, that would be to mistake lethargy for strategy.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Very droll, Humphrey, but you must realise that there is a real desire for radical reform in the air. The all-party Select Committee on Administrative Affairs, which I founded, was a case in point. It's a great success.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Oh, indeed. What has it achieved?

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Nothing yet, but the party's very pleased with it.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Why?

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Ten column inches in last Monday's Daily Mail for a start.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Oh, I see. The government is going to measure its success in column inches, is it?

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Yes, no. Yes and no! [Sits down in his chair off camera]

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Minister, the evidence that you're proposing to submit is not only untrue, it is also, which is much more serious, unwise. Now, we've been through all this before. The expansion of the Civil Service is the result of parliamentary legislation, not bureaucratic empire building.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: So when this next comes up in Question Time, you want me to tell Parliament that it's their fault that the Civil Service is too big?

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: But it's the truth, Minister.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: I don't want the truth! I want something I can tell Parliament! Humphrey, you're my permanent secretary, you're supposed to enact my policies. Yet, I still don't understand why you seem implacably opposed to them. I must know where you stand on all this.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Where one stands, Minister, depends upon where one sits.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Am I to infer that you'll not support me?

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Oh, we'll always support you, Minister; but as your standard bearer, not as your pallbearer.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Humphrey, What are you saying?

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: I should have thought it was crystal clear, Minister. Do not send this report to a body whose recommendations are to be published!

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: That is exactly why I'm sending it. Now I don't want to hear any more about it.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: May I say just one more thing?

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Only if it's in plain English!

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Very well, Minister: if you're going to do this damn silly thing, don't do it in this damn silly way.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Minister, Britain has had the same foreign policy objective for at least the last five hundred years: to create a disunited Europe. In that cause we have fought with the Dutch against the Spanish, with the Germans against the French, with the French and Italians against the Germans, and with the French against the Germans and Italians. Divide and rule, you see. Why should we change now, when it's worked so well?

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: That's all ancient history, surely?

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Yes, and current policy. We had to break the whole thing [the EEC] up, so we had to get inside. We tried to break it up from the outside, but that wouldn't work. Now that we're inside we can make a complete pig's breakfast of the whole thing — set the Germans against the French, the French against the Italians, the Italians against the Dutch... The Foreign Office is terribly pleased; it's just like old times.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: But surely we're all committed to the European ideal?

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: [chuckles] Really, Minister.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: If not, why are we pushing for an increase in the membership?

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Well, for the same reason. It's just like the United Nations, in fact; the more members it has, the more arguments it can stir up, the more futile and impotent it becomes.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: What appalling cynicism.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Yes... We call it diplomacy, Minister.
The Foreign Secretary explains the Napoleon prize.

lines.speaker: Martin
lines.text: Yes, it's a NATO award given once every five years: gold medal, big ceremony in Brussels, £100 000. The PM's the front runner this time. It's for the statesman who's made the biggest contribution to European unity.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Since Napoleon. That is if you don't count Hitler.

lines.speaker: Daniel Hughes
lines.text: Let's face it, all your functions could be subsumed by other departments. Jim Hacker will win through with a thoroughly public-spirited, self-sacrificing policy. The PM will probably kick him upstairs: Lord Hacker of Kamikaze. [chuckles]

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: I hardly think that's funny, Daniel. Or likely.

lines.speaker: Daniel Hughes
lines.text: But why not? I mean, he ran the leadership campaign against the PM, didn't he? This could be the PM's masterstroke! In one fell swoop: approbation, elevation, and castration. You know the PM's motto: in defeat, malice. In victory, revenge.

episodes.title: The Right to Know
episodes.titleFull: Episode Six: The Right to Know

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Humphrey, do you see it as part of your job to help ministers make fools of themselves?

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Well, I never met one that needed any help.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Minister, I have something to say to you which you may not like to hear.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Why should today be any different?

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Minister, the traditional allocation of executive responsibilities has always been so determined as to liberate the ministerial incumbent from the administrative minutiae by devolving the managerial functions to those whose experience and qualifications have better formed them for the performance of such humble offices, thereby releasing their political overlords for the more onerous duties and profound deliberations which are the inevitable concomitant of their exalted position.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: I wonder what made you think I didn't want to hear that?
How to guide ministers to making the right decisions

lines.speaker: Sir Frederick
lines.text: [...] there are four words to be included in a proposal if you want it thrown out.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Complicated. Lengthy. Expensive. Controversial. And if you want to be really sure that the Minister doesn't accept it, you must say the decision is "courageous".

lines.speaker: Bernard
lines.text: And that's worse than "controversial"?

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Oh, yes! "Controversial" only means "this will lose you votes". "Courageous" means "this will lose you the election"!
While going through the Minister's post

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: You know the rules, Bernard - if it is not marked "Private and Confidential" we are obliged to open it.

lines.speaker: Bernard
lines.text: What if it's marked "Daddy"?
Humphrey tries to explain about Lucy's nude protest

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: The Minister's daughter is to be...that is to say, she will not be...

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Come on Humphrey, make a clean breast of it!

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: An unfortunate turn of phrase, Minister.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: One: I am not a "badger-butcher". Two: badgers are not an endangered species. Three: the removal of protective status does not necessarily mean the badgers will be killed. Four: if a few badgers have to be sacrificed for the sake of a master plan that will save Britain's natural heritage - tough!

lines.speaker: Lucy
lines.text: [sarcastically gives a Nazi salute] Ze "master plan", mein Fuhrer! Ze end justifies ze means, does it?!
After Sir Humphrey prevents Lucy's nude protest by telling her that the Hayward Spinney badger colony is non-existent

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Humphrey, was there one word of truth in that whole story that you told Lucy?

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Minister, do you really want me to answer that question?

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: [thinks uneasily] No, I don't think I do.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: [smiles] Quite so. Perhaps there are some things it is better for a Minister not to know?

episodes.title: Jobs for the Boys
episodes.titleFull: Episode Seven: Jobs for the Boys

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Bernard, Ministers should never know more than they need to know. Then they can't tell anyone. Like secret agents; they could be captured and tortured.

lines.speaker: Bernard
lines.text: [shocked] You mean by terrorists?

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: [seriously] By the BBC, Bernard.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: You're blathering, Bernard.

lines.speaker: Bernard
lines.text: Yes, Minister.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Why are you blathering, Bernard?

lines.speaker: Bernard
lines.text: It's my job, Minister.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: It takes two to quango, Minister!

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: The National Health Service, Humphrey, is an advanced case of galloping bureaucracy!

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Oh, certainly not galloping. A gentle canter at the most.
Sir Humphrey agrees with the union leader that industrial action at St Edward's Hospital would also benefit civil servants.

lines.speaker: Brian Baker
lines.text: What about the Minister?

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: The Minister doesn't know his Acas from his NALGO.
Hacker is reading some paperwork in his office when Sir Humphrey enters

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Good Morning, Minister. Morning, Bernard.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Humphrey.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Er, two things, Minister. The first, this matter of the departmental recommendations for the honours list.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Oh, the honours list again!

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Yes, Minister.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Well, I think we'll leave that for the moment, Humphrey, shall we?.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: I don't think we can leave it, Minister. (Hands the papers back to Hacker) It's getting dangerously near the five weeks.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Five weeks?

lines.speaker: Bernard
lines.text: Oh, yes. All recipients are notified at least five weeks before prorogation. It gives them time to refuse, you know.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: When did a civil servant last refuse an honour?!

lines.speaker: Bernard
lines.text: Well I think there was somebody in the Treasury that refused a knighthood.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Good God. When?

lines.speaker: Bernard
lines.text: I think it was 1496.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Why?

lines.speaker: Bernard
lines.text: He'd already got one.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Well, Minister, if you've approved the list...

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Humphrey, did you know that 20% of all honours go to civil servants?

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: A fitting tribute to their devotion to duty, Minister.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: No, their duty is what they get paid for. The rest of the population has to do something extra to get an honour. Something special. They work for 27 years with mentally handicapped children six nights a week to get an MBE. Your knighthoods simply come up with the rations.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Minister, her Majesty's civil servants spend their lives working for a modest wage and at the end, they retire into obscurity. Honours are a small reward for a lifetime of loyal, self-effacing discretion and devoted service to Her Majesty, and to the nation.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: "A modest wage", did you say?

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Alas, yes.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Humphrey, you get over £30,000 a year! That's £7,000 more than I get.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Yes, but still relatively the modest wage.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Relative to whom?

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Well, Elizabeth Taylor, for example.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Humphrey, you are not relative to Elizabeth Taylor. There are important differences.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Indeed, yes. She didn't get a first at Oxford.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: And you do not retire into obscurity?! You take a massive index-linked pension and go off to become directors of oil companies and banks.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Oh, yes, but very obscure directors, Minister.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: You're in no danger of the sack. In industry if you screw things up, you get the boot. In the civil service, if you screw things up, I get the boot.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Very droll, Minister, now if you've approved the list...

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: No, Humphrey. I'm not going to approve any honour for any civil servant of this department who hasn't earned it.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: What do you mean "earned it?"

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: I mean "earned it." Done something to deserve it.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: [outraged] But that's unheard of!

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: My new policy is to withhold all honours from all civil servants in this department who do not make a cut in their budgets of 5% per year. May I take it that your silence indicates approval?

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: You may not! Where did you get that preposterous idea?

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: It, uh... just came to me.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: But it's ridiculous! It's unheard of! It's out of the question!

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Why?

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: But the whole idea is... it it it it it... It's... It strikes at the very roots of... It's the beginning of the end! The thin end of the wedge! A Bennite solution! Where will it end? The abolition of the monarchy?

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Don't be absurd, Humphrey.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: There is no reason to change the system which has worked so well in the past.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: But it hasn't.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: But we've got to give the present system a fair trial.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Ah, yes, I thought you might say that. It may interest you to know, Humphrey, that the Most Noble Order of the Garter was founded in 1348 by King Edward III. I think perhaps it may be coming towards the end of its trial period now, don't you?

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Minister, if you block honours pending economies, you might create a dangerous precedent.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: You mean that if we do the right thing this time, we might have to do the right thing again next time? Nothing would ever get done at all!

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: On the contrary, many, many things must be done, but...

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Nothing must be done for the first time! Don't...

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: No, Minister! What I mean is that I am fully seized of your aims, and of course I will do my utmost to see that they're put into practice.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: If you would.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: To that end, I recommend that we set up an interdepartmental committee with fairly broad terms of reference, so that at the end of the day, we'll be in a position to think through the various implications and arrive at a decision based on long-term considerations rather than rush prematurely into precipitate and possibly ill-conceived actions which might well have unforeseen repercussions.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: You mean "no"?

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: I mean, as far as one can see, in the fullness of time, looking at...

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: No, no, no, no, Humphrey. You know me: Action now!

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: [mutters] Action now.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Nobody in their right mind can want honours. They encourage sycophancy, snobbery, jealousy, and it's not fair civil servants shouldn't get them all!

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: But, Minister...

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: No, no! I'm - I'm sorry, Humphrey, I have decided. What was your other point?

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Other point?

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: You had two.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Did I? Yes, I'm sorry. The shock! Yes. Minister, Yesterday, I had representations from Baillie College, Oxford. A new ruling about grants for overseas students. Now Baillie stands to lose nearly a quarter of a £1,000,000 a year.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: They must just take more British students.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: I'm sure nothing would please them more, Minister, but you see, Baillie has quite easily the highest proportion of foreign students, and there could be very serious repercussions at the schools of tropical medicine, and international law, and the Arabic department might have to close down completely.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: I'm sorry, we simply can't go on educating foreigners at the taxpayer's expense.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Well it's not just foreigners, you know, Minister, if the diplomatic service had nowhere to immerse its recruits in Arab culture, for example, the results could be catastrophic. We might even end up with a pro-Israeli Foreign Office! And what would happen to our oil policy then?

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: You just have to immerse its recruits elsewhere.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Where else would they learn Arabic?

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Arabia?

lines.speaker: Bernard
lines.text: Actually, Minister, Baillie College does have an outstanding record. It's filled the jails in the British Empire for many years.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: [off camera] Jails?

lines.speaker: Bernard
lines.text: Yes indeed. As you know, the letters "JB" are the most outstanding honour in the Commonwealth.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: "JB"?

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: "Jailed by the British". Gandhi, Nkrumah, Makarios, Ben Gurion, Kenyatta, Nehru, Mugabe, the list of world leaders is endless, and contains several of our students.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: "Our students"? Humphrey, which college did you go to?

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: That's quite beside the point!

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: But I like being beside the point. Humour me, Humphrey. Which college did you go to?

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: It so happens that I am a Baillie man, but that has nothing to do with it!

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Oh, of course not! What a thought! [slaps wrist] Naughty!
The telephone sounds and Bernard answers it

lines.speaker: Bernard
lines.text: Yes? (to Hacker) Oh. it's the division, Minister.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Well, that rather settles it, doesn't it, Humphrey? (Gets out of his chair) No more time. (Gives his paperwork to Bernard) Oh, Bernard, which am I supposed to be voting, "aye" or "no"?

lines.speaker: Bernard
lines.text: "No". It's an opposition, it's the second reading...

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: I don't want to know what it is. I don't want to go through the wrong door. (He goes over to the door as Bernard throws his paperwork back on the desk)
Bernard explains to the Minister the honours available to senior Civil Servants.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Well, what has Sir Arnold to fear, anyway? He's got all the honours he could want, surely?

lines.speaker: Bernard
lines.text: Well, naturally he has his G.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: G?

lines.speaker: Bernard
lines.text: Yes; you get your G after your K.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: You speak in riddles, Bernard.

lines.speaker: Bernard
lines.text: Well, take the Foreign Office. First you get the CMG, then the KCMG, then the GCMG; the Commander of the Order of St Michael and St George, Knight Commander of St Michael and St George, Knight Grand Cross of St Michael and St George. Of course, in the Service, CMG stands for "Call Me God," and KCMG for "Kindly Call Me God."

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: [chuckles] What does GCMG stand for?

lines.speaker: Bernard
lines.text: "God Calls Me God."
The Master of Baillie College learns why the honorary doctorate of law should not go to a judge.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: [a bit drunk] A judge?! You don't want to make a judge a doctor of laws! Politicians are the ones who make the laws, and pass the laws! If it wasn't for politicians, judges wouldn't be able to do any judging! They wouldn't have any laws to judge! They'd all be out of work! There'd be queues of unemployed judges! In silly wigs!

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: [tries to interrupt] I think what the Minister is trying to say is...

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Besides, it's easy for judges. Judges don't have to lie to television producers, don't have to suck up to journalists, don't have to pretend they like their Cabinet colleagues. Do you know something? Well I'll tell you: if judges had to put up with some of my Cabinet colleagues, they'd bring capital punishment back tomorrow! Bloody good thing, too!

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: [tries to interrupt] Well, exactly, Minister...

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: And I'll tell you another thing: I can't send him [points at Sir Humphrey] to prison. Can't send him to prison! Now, if I were a judge, I could whiz old Humpy off to The Scrubs, no trouble. Feet wouldn't touch. Clang, bang, see you in three years' time! One-third remission for good conduct. But I can't do that! I have to listen to him! Oh, God! On and on and on! Do you know, some of his sentences are longer than Judge Jeffreys'! No, you don't want to make a judge a doctor of laws.
Stunned pause

lines.speaker: Master of Baillie College
lines.text: Beautifully argued, Minister.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: What does "egregious" mean?

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Um, I think it means outstanding... In one way or another.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Ask Walter Fowler of The Express to meet me in the House tonight for a drink. Annie's bar.

lines.speaker: Bernard
lines.text: What for, Minister?

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: First law of political indiscretion: always have a drink before you leak.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: The freedom of the British people is worth more than the lives of a few Ministers. Freedom is indivisible. Ministers are expendable. A man in public life must expect to be the target of cranks and fanatics. [Sliding into a Churchill impersonation.] It is a Minister's duty to set his life at naught. He must be able to stand up and say, here I am, do your worst! And not cower in craven terror behind electronic equipment, secret microphones, and all the hideous apparatus of the police state. [He snaps back to his normal self.] Anyway, Humphrey, I don't want to hear any more about it.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: But Minister, you must allow me to say just one more thing on this matter.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Very well, just one, but be brief.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: The Special Branch have found your name on a death list.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: That has absolutely no bearing on the situation... What?!
Bernard wheels in a petition from the archives against surveillance, containing more than two million signatures.

lines.speaker: Bernard
lines.text: Shall I file it?

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Shall you file it? Shred it!

lines.speaker: Bernard
lines.text: Shred it?

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: No one must ever be able to find it again!

lines.speaker: Bernard
lines.text: In that case, Minister, I think it's best I file it.
Sir Humphrey informs the Minister that the Special Branch no longer believe there is a threat to the Minister's life.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: How do they know?

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Surveillance. They overheard a conversation.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: What did it say?

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Oh I don't think it's of any particular—

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: [Interrupting] Come on, Humphrey! I have a right to know!

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Well, it was a conversation to the effect that in view of the somewhat nebulous and inexplicit nature of your remit, and the arguably marginal and peripheral nature of your influence within the central deliberations and decisions within the political process, there could be a case for restructuring their action priorities in such a way as to eliminate your liquidation from their immediate agenda.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: They said that?

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: That was the gist of it.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: What does it mean? In English?!

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Well, it means that they don't think you're really important enough for it to be worth assassinating you.
No one at the meeting seems to know anything about chemistry.

lines.speaker: Joan Littler
lines.text: What does "inert" mean?

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Well it means it's not… ert.

lines.speaker: Bernard
lines.text: [to himself] Wouldn't ert a fly.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Minister, a minister can do what he likes!

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: It's the people's will. I am their leader; I must follow them.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: The people are ignorant and misguided.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Humphrey, it's the people who elected me.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: [smiles and nods]

episodes.title: The Devil You Know
episodes.titleFull: Episode Five: The Devil You Know

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Europe is a community of nations, dedicated towards one goal.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: [laughs moderately]

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: May we share the joke, Humphrey?

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Oh Minister, let's look at this objectively. It is a game played for national interests, and always was. Why do you suppose we went into it?

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: To strengthen the brotherhood of free Western nations.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Oh really. We went in to screw the French by splitting them off from the Germans.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: So why did the French go into it, then?

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Well, to protect their inefficient farmers from commercial competition.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: That certainly doesn't apply to the Germans.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: No, no. They went in to cleanse themselves of genocide and apply for readmission to the human race.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: I never heard such appalling cynicism! At least the small nations didn't go into it for selfish reasons.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Oh really? Luxembourg is in it for the perks; the capital of the EEC, all that foreign money pouring in.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Very sensible central location.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: With the administration in Brussels and the Parliament in Strasbourg? Minister, it's like having the House of Commons in Swindon and the Civil Service in Kettering!
The Minister and his subordinates discuss the rumoured Cabinet reshuffle.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: How does Basil Corbett know about it when we don't?

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Perhaps he has the PM's ear.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Yes, he is in the PM's pocket.

lines.speaker: Bernard
lines.text: Then the PM must have rather a large ear.
Sir Humphrey claims he would be deeply sorry to see the Minister leave the DAA.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Yes, I suppose we have got rather fond of one another. In a way.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: [laughs] In a way, yes!

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: [jokingly] Like a terrorist and his hostage!

lines.speaker: Bernard
lines.text: Which one of you is the terrorist?

lines.speaker: Hacker & Sir Humphrey
lines.text: [each points at the other] He is.

episodes.title: The Quality of Life
episodes.titleFull: Episode Six: The Quality of Life

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Didn't you read the Financial Times this morning?

lines.speaker: Sir Desmond
lines.text: Never do.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Well, you're a banker. Surely you read the Financial Times?

lines.speaker: Sir Desmond
lines.text: Can't understand it. Full of economic theory.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Why do you buy it?

lines.speaker: Sir Desmond
lines.text: Oh, you know, it's part of the uniform. It took me thirty years to understand Keynes' economics. Then when I'd just cottoned on, everyone started getting hooked on these new monetarist ideas, you know, 'I Want To Be Free' by Milton Shulman.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Milton Friedman.

lines.speaker: Sir Desmond
lines.text: Why are they all called Milton? Anyway, I've only got as far as Milton Keynes.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Maynard Keynes.

lines.speaker: Sir Desmond
lines.text: I'm sure there's a Milton Keynes.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Yes, there is, but it's... [Humphrey gives up]

episodes.title: A Question of Loyalty
episodes.titleFull: Episode Seven: A Question of Loyalty

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Why is it that ministers can't ever go anywhere without their briefs?

lines.speaker: Bernard
lines.text: It's in case they get caught with their trousers down.
Standard excuses when faced with serious allegations

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: There's the excuse we used for the Munich Agreement: it occurred before certain important facts were known and couldn't happen again.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: What important facts?

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Well, that Hitler wanted to conquer Europe.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: I thought everybody knew that.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Not the Foreign Office.
Why has the Minister been invited to Number 10?

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Perhaps it is just for a drink, Minister.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Don't be silly, Humphrey. They don't ask you to Number 10 for a drink just because they think you're thirsty!

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: It's not for me to comment on government policy. You must ask the Minister.

lines.speaker: Betty Oldham
lines.text: Look, Sir Humphrey, whatever we ask the Minister, he says is an administrative question for you, and whatever we ask you, you say is a policy question for the Minister. How do you suggest we find out what is going on?

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Yes, yes, yes, I do see that there is a real dilemma here. In that, while it has been government policy to regard policy as a responsibility of Ministers and administration as a responsibility of Officials, the questions of administrative policy can cause confusion between the policy of administration and the administration of policy, especially when responsibility for the administration of the policy of administration conflicts, or overlaps with, responsibility for the policy of the administration of policy.

lines.speaker: Betty Oldham
lines.text: Well, that's a load of meaningless drivel. [pause] Isn't it?

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: It's not for me to comment on government policy. You must ask the Minister.
How to deal with a nonsensical complaint

lines.speaker: Bernard
lines.text: We can CGSM it.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: CGSM?

lines.speaker: Bernard
lines.text: Civil Service code, Minister. It stands for "Consignment of Geriatric Shoe Manufacturers".

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: What?

lines.speaker: Bernard
lines.text: A load of old cobblers, Minister.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: I'm not a civil servant. I shall use my own code. I shall write: "Round Objects".
...later...

lines.speaker: Bernard
lines.text: You remember that letter you wrote "Round Objects" on?

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Oh yes.

lines.speaker: Bernard
lines.text: It's come back from Sir Humphrey's office. He's commented on it.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: What does he say?

lines.speaker: Bernard
lines.text: Who is Round and to what does he object?

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Now, Minister, if you are going to promote women just because they're the best person for the job, you will create a lot of resentment throughout the whole of the Civil Service!

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: The three articles of Civil Service faith: it takes longer to do things quickly, it's more expensive to do them cheaply and it's more democratic to do them in secret.

lines.speaker: Sir Arnold
lines.text: Life is so much easier when ministers think they've achieved something; it stops them fretting, and their little temper tantrums.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Yes, but now he wants to introduce his next idea.

lines.speaker: Sir Arnold
lines.text: A minister with two ideas? I can't remember when we last had one of those.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: [talking about nuclear fallout shelters] Well, you have the weapons; you must have the shelters.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: I sometimes wonder why we need the weapons.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Minister! You're not a unilateralist?

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: I sometimes wonder, you know.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Well, then, you must resign from the government!

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Ah, no, no, no, no, no, no, no. I'm not that unilateralist! Anyway, the Americans will always protect us from the Russians, won't they?

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Russians? Who's talking about the Russians?

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Well, the independent deterrent.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: It's to protect us against the French!

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: The French?! But that's astounding!

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Why?

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Well they're our allies, our partners.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Well, they are now, but they've been our enemies for the most of the past 900 years. If they've got the bomb, we must have the bomb!

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: If it's for the French, of course, that's different. Makes a lot of sense.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Yes. Can't trust the Frogs.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: You can say that again!

episodes.title: The Skeleton in the Cupboard
episodes.titleFull: Episode Three: The Skeleton in the Cupboard

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: If local authorities don't send us statistics, Government figures will be a nonsense.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Why?

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: They'll be incomplete.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Government figures are a nonsense, anyway.

lines.speaker: Bernard
lines.text: I think Sir Humphrey wants to ensure they're a complete nonsense.

lines.speaker: Bernard
lines.text: [on the phone] Hello, Graham, it's Bernard. Tell Sir Humphrey that the Minister's just gone walkabout. Yes, yes, AWOL. Well, of course I told him, yes. I know. I think you'd better let him know right away.
hangs up

lines.speaker: Bernard
lines.text: One... two... three... four... five... six... seven... eight... nine... TEN.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: [walks in on the stroke of ten] What's all this about?

lines.speaker: Bernard
lines.text: The minister's just left the office, that's all.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: That's all? Do you mean he's loose in the building? Why didn't you warn me?

lines.speaker: Bernard
lines.text: I did advise him, but he is the minister. There's no prohibition against ministers talking to their staff.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Who's he talking to?

lines.speaker: Bernard
lines.text: Perhaps he was just restless.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: If the minister's restless, he can feed the ducks in St James's Park!

lines.speaker: Bernard
lines.text: Yes, Sir Humphrey.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Tell me who the minister's talking to.

lines.speaker: Bernard
lines.text: Well, surely the minister can talk to anyone?

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Bernard... I'm in the middle of writing your annual report. Now, it is not a responsibility that either of us would wish me to discharge whilst I am in a bad temper. Who's the minister talking to?

lines.speaker: Bernard
lines.text: Perhaps you could help me. I can see that you should know if he calls on an outsider. I fail to see why you should be informed if he just wants to, to take a hypothetical example, to check a point with... Dr Cartwright...

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Thank you, Bernard. Must fly.

lines.speaker: Bernard
lines.text: Room 4017.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: I know!

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Bernard, how did Sir Humphrey know I was with Dr Cartwright?

lines.speaker: Bernard
lines.text: God moves in a mysterious way.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Let me make one thing perfectly clear: Humphrey is not God, OK?

lines.speaker: Bernard
lines.text: Will you tell him or shall I?

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Get Humphrey to come back here at once.

lines.speaker: Bernard
lines.text: Yes, Minister. [Picks up phone] The Minister wonders if Sir Humphrey could spare time for a meeting sometime in the next few days.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: At once.

lines.speaker: Bernard
lines.text: In fact, sometime today is really...

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: At once!

lines.speaker: Bernard
lines.text: ...Sometime during the next 60 seconds. [hangs up] He's coming round now.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Why? Did he faint?

lines.speaker: Bernard
lines.text: No, he's just, you know...
they both start giggling

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: This is serious, Bernard.

lines.speaker: Bernard
lines.text: Yes, I know.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: This is no laughing matter.

lines.speaker: Bernard
lines.text: No, certainly not.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: The question is, how am I going to deal with it?

lines.speaker: Bernard
lines.text: In my opinion...

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: The question was purely rhetorical, Bernard.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: The identity of the official whose alleged responsibility for this hypothetical oversight has been the subject of recent discussion is not shrouded in quite such impenetrable obscurity as certain previous disclosures may have led you to assume; but not to put too fine a point on it, the individual in question is, it may surprise you to learn, one whom your present interlocutor is in the habit of defining by means of the perpendicular pronoun.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: I beg your pardon?

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: It was... I.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: How am I going to explain the missing documents to the Mail?

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Well, this is what we normally do in circumstances like these.
passes Hacker a memo

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: "This file contains the complete set of papers, except for a number of secret documents, a few others which are part of still active files, some correspondence lost in the floods of 1967..." Was 1967 a particularly bad winter?

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: No, a marvellous winter. We lost no end of embarrassing files.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: "...Some records which went astray in the move to London and others when the War Office was incorporated in the Ministry of Defence, and the normal withdrawal of papers whose publication could give grounds for an action for libel or breach of confidence or cause embarrassment to friendly governments". That's pretty comprehensive. How many does that normally leave for them to look at?

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: How many does it actually leave? About a hundred?... Fifty?... Ten?... Five?... Four?... Three?... Two?... One?... Zero?

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Yes, Minister.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Well, obviously I'm not a trained lawyer or I wouldn't have been in charge of the legal unit!

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Isn't this terrible? Print baseless accusations like this!

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Oh, yes, yes, terrible.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Baksheesh, palm-greasing! Good God, we're British!

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Absolutely, Minister!

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Still, it's not like the FT to print a story like this unless there's something behind it. Is there something behind it, Humphrey?

lines.speaker: Bernard
lines.text: I think the sports news is behind it.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: I want to know the truth, Humphrey.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: I don't think you do, Minister.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Will you answer a direct question?

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: I strongly advise you not to ask a direct question.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Why?

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: It might provoke a direct answer.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: It never has yet.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Bernard, what do YOU know about this? Tell me on your word of honour.

lines.speaker: Bernard
lines.text: Oh, well, I... er... Er, that is... there was. Someone did.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: It’s a lot of gossip, that's all. Rumour, hearsay.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Bernard?

lines.speaker: Bernard
lines.text: Well one of the Kumranis did tell me he'd received...

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Hearsay, Minister.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Hearsay?

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Yes, Bernard heard him say it.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Are you telling me Humphrey that the BES contract was won by bribery?

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Oh Minister, I do wish you wouldn't use words like bribery.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: What would you like me to say? Slush funds, sweeteners, brown envelopes?

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Oh Minister these are extremely crude and unworthy expressions for what is no more than creative negotiation. It is the general practice.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: You do realise what you're saying don’t you, Humphrey? I ratified that contract, didn’t I? In good faith!

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Yes indeed, Minister.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: And in that communiqué I issued to the press, I announced a British success won in a fair fight!

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Mm, yes, I did wonder about that bit.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Now you're telling me it was got by bribery.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: No, Minister.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Oh, it was not got by bribery?

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: That is not what I said.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: What did you say?

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: I said I'm not telling you it was got by bribery.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Well how would you describe these payments?

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: How does the contract describe them you mean? Oh, well, that's really quite simple. Retainers, personal donations, special discounts. Miscellaneous outgoings, agents' fees, political contributions, management expenses.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: And how are these payments made?

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Well anything from a numbered account in a Swiss bank, to a fistful of used oncers slipped under the door of the gents.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Are you saying that winking at corruption is government policy?

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: No, no, Minister! It could never be government policy. That is unthinkable! Only government practice.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: You're a cynic, Humphrey!

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: A cynic is what an idealist calls a realist.

episodes.title: The Bed of Nails
episodes.titleFull: Episode Five: The Bed of Nails

lines.text: Hacker has been offered the job of Transport Supremo.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Sir Mark thinks there might be votes in it, and I do not intend to look a gift horse in the mouth.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: I put it to you, Minister, that you are looking a Trojan horse in the mouth.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: You mean if we look closely at this gift horse, we'll find it's full of Trojans?

lines.speaker: Bernard
lines.text: Um, if you had looked the Trojan Horse in the mouth, Minister, you would have found Greeks inside. Well, the point is that it was the Greeks who gave the Trojan horse to the Trojans, so technically it wasn't a Trojan horse at all; it was a Greek horse. Hence the tag "timeo Danaos et dona ferentes", which, you will recall, is usually and somewhat inaccurately translated as "beware of Greeks bearing gifts", or doubtless you would have recalled had you not attended the LSE.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Yes, well, I'm sure Greek tags are all very well in their way; but can we stick to the point?

lines.speaker: Bernard
lines.text: Sorry, sorry: Greek tags?

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: "Beware of Greeks bearing gifts." I suppose the EEC equivalent would be "Beware of Greeks bearing an olive oil surplus".

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Excellent, Minister.

lines.speaker: Bernard
lines.text: No, well, the point is, Minister, that just as the Trojan horse was in fact Greek, what you describe as a Greek tag is in fact Latin. It's obvious, really: the Greeks would never suggest bewaring of themselves, if one can use such a participle (bewaring that is). And it's clearly Latin, not because timeo ends in "-o", because the Greek first person also ends in "-o" – although actually there is a Greek word timao, meaning 'I honour'. But the "-os" ending is a nominative singular termination of a second declension in Greek, and an accusative plural in Latin, of course, though actually Danaos is not only the Greek for 'Greek'; it's also the Latin for 'Greek'. It's very interesting, really.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: The ship of state, Bernard, is the only ship that leaks from the top.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Last night a confidential source disclosed to me that British arms are being sold to Italian red terrorist groups.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: I see. May I ask who this confidential source was?

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Humphrey, I just said it was confidential.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Oh, I'm sorry. I naturally assumed that meant you were going to tell me.

lines.speaker: Bernard
lines.text: So what do we believe in?

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: At this moment, Bernard, we believe in stopping the minister from informing the Prime Minister.

lines.speaker: Bernard
lines.text: But why?

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Because once the Prime Minister knows, there will have to be an enquiry, like Watergate. The investigation of a trivial break-in led to one ghastly revelation after another and finally the downfall of a president. The golden rule is don't lift lids off cans of worms. Everything is connected to everything else. Who said that?

lines.speaker: Bernard
lines.text: The Cabinet Secretary?

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Nearly right. Actually, it was Lenin.

lines.speaker: Bernard
lines.text: How do you stop a Cabinet Minister talking to a Prime Minister?

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Interesting question. You tell me.

lines.speaker: Bernard
lines.text: I don't know.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Work it out. You're supposed to be a high flier. Or are you really a low-flier supported by occasional gusts of wind?
The Minister has received a letter with information about sanctions violations.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: I'm trapped. I can't tell the PM, I can't not tell the PM.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: I see.

lines.speaker: Bernard
lines.text: I was just wondering, Minister, if we may not use the Rhodesia solution.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Bernard! You excel yourself! Of course, Minister, the Rhodesia solution!

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: What are you talking about?

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Oil sanctions, remember? A member of the government was told about the way British companies were sanction-busting.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: What did you do?

lines.speaker: Bernard
lines.text: He told the Prime Minister.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: What did he do?

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: He told the Prime Minister in such a way that the Prime Minister didn't hear him.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Would you mean I should mumble it or something in the division lobby?

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: No, Minister, you write a note.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: In very faint pencil? Please, be practical.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: No, Minister, it's awfully obvious; you write a note which is susceptible to misinterpretation.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Oh, I see. Dear Prime Minister, it has come to my attention that the Italian Red Terrorists are getting hold of British top secret bomb-making equipment—how do you misinterpret that?

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: You can't.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Well, exactly.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: So you don't write that. You use a more circumspect style, and you avoid any mention of bombs, or terrorists, or any of that.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Wouldn't that be rather difficult? Is that what it's all about?

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: You say—Bernard, write this down—My attention has been drawn, on a personal basis, to information which suggests the possibility of certain irregularities under Section... [snaps fingers]

lines.speaker: Bernard
lines.text: Section 1 of the Import, Export and Customs Powers Defence Act 1939 C.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Thank you, Bernard. You then go on to suggest that somebody else should do something about it. Prima facie evidence suggests that there could be a case for further investigation; to establish whether or not enquiries should be put in hand. And then you smudge it all over.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Nevertheless, it should be stressed that available information is limited, and relevant facts could be difficult to establish with any degree of certainty.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: I see.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Then, if there were an inquiry, you'd be in the clear, and everybody would understand that the busy PM might not have grasped the full implications of such a letter

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: They certainly would; that's most unclear.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Thank you, Minister. Then you arrange for the letter to arrive at Number 10 on the day the PM leaves for an overseas summit, so there's also doubt about whether it was the PM or the acting PM who read the note. And so the whole thing is written off as a breakdown in communications, everybody's in the clear, and everybody can get on with their business.

lines.speaker: Bernard
lines.text: Including the Red Terrorists.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Exactly.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: My job is to carry out government policy.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Even if you think it's wrong?

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Well, almost all government policy is wrong, but… frightfully well carried out.

lines.speaker: Bernard
lines.text: If it's our job to carry out government policies, shouldn't we believe in them?

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Oh, what an extraordinary idea! I have served 11 governments in the past 30 years. If I'd believed in all their policies, I'd have been passionately committed to keeping out of the Common Market, and passionately committed to joining it. I'd have been utterly convinced of the rightness of nationalising steel and of denationalising it and renationalising it. Capital punishment? I'd have been a fervent retentionist and an ardent abolitionist. I'd have been a Keynesian and a Friedmanite, a grammar school preserver and destroyer, a nationalisation freak and a privatisation maniac, but above all, I would have been a stark-staring raving schizophrenic!

lines.speaker: Bernard
lines.text: So they are, railway trains are impartial too, but if you lay down the lines for them that's the way they go.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: [calmly] Bernard, subsidy is for art, for culture. [almost furiously] It is not to be given to what the people want! It is for what the people don't want but ought to have!

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Nothing wrong with subsidising sport. Sport is educational.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: We have sex education too. Should we subsidise sex, perhaps?

lines.speaker: Bernard
lines.text: [earnestly] Oh, could we?

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: In addition to your existing responsibilities, you will be Cabinet Minister responsible for the Arts.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: [smiling] Eh? I say, that's rather good, isn't it? Hold on -- how do you know about this before I do?

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Oh, I just happened to be with the Cabinet Secretary shortly after the decision was taken.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: [pleased] Cabinet Minister with the responsibility for the Arts, eh? Well well well!

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Yes indeed!

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Thank you for letting me know, Humphrey! Anything more? I'm just about to start a meeting.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Oh, the meeting, yes. Now Minister, I do hope that you've considered the implications of your new appointment on the subject you're discussing.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: What, rescuing a football club?

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: No, no, no; I was wondering how it would look if, as Cabinet Minister responsible for the Arts, your first action would be to knock down an art gallery.

lines.speaker: Councillor Brian Wilkinson
lines.text: I can't believe this! You mean I've got to go and tell the people back home that you've gone back on your word? I mean, it was your own idea!

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: I mean, it's not me, it's the law!

lines.speaker: Councillor Brian Wilkinson
lines.text: Well, why didn't you find out until now?

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Well, um--
Bernard coughs, attracting the Minister's attention, and keeps glancing at the paperwork for increased allowances for councillors, until Hacker finally gets the hint

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: [taking the paperwork in hand] Let me be absolutely frank with you. The truth is, it would be possible to push this through. Just possible. But it would take an awful long time.

lines.speaker: Councillor Brian Wilkinson
lines.text: Okay, take the time! We've spent enough!

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Yes, but the trouble is, you see, something else would have to go by the board. And the thing that's taking my time at the moment is forcing through this increase in councillor's expenses and attendance allowances. You see, I can't put my personal weight behind both schemes. I suppose I could forget about the increased allowances for councillors...
Wilkinson and his fellow councillors look at each other, alarmed

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: ...concentrate on the legal obstacles to the sale of the art gallery.

lines.speaker: Councillor Brian Wilkinson
lines.text: [in a less confrontational tone] Tricky things, legal obstacles.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: And this is a particularly tricky one.

lines.speaker: Councillor Brian Wilkinson
lines.text: And at the end of the day, you might still fail.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Every possibility.

lines.speaker: Councillor Brian Wilkinson
lines.text: Well, if that's the way it is... [turns to one of his fellow councillors] There is a chance that we might want to close Edgehill Road Primary at the end of the year. That site should fetch a couple of million, give or take.
the councillors rise from their chairs

lines.speaker: Councillor Brian Wilkinson
lines.text: Well, there it is, then! No ill feelings, Jim! [shakes hands with the Minister]

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Good! And you'll explain locally that we can't overcome the legal obstacles?

lines.speaker: Councillor Brian Wilkinson
lines.text: Of course we will!
Councillor Wilkinson points at the paperwork regarding increased allowances for councillors

lines.speaker: Councillor Brian Wilkinson
lines.text: Ah, carry on with the good work, eh?
the councillors depart

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Oh, Minister...a work of art.

episodes.title: Christmas at the Ministry (1982): "The Funny Side of Christmas"
episodes.titleFull: Christmas at the Ministry (1982): "The Funny Side of Christmas"

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: I wonder if I might crave your momentary indulgence in order to discharge a by no means disagreeable obligation which has, over the years, become more or less established practice in government service as we approach the terminal period of the year — calendar, of course, not financial — in fact, not to put too fine a point on it, Week Fifty-One — and submit to you, with all appropriate deference, for your consideration at a convenient juncture, a sincere and sanguine expectation — indeed confidence — indeed one might go so far as to say hope — that the aforementioned period may be, at the end of the day, when all relevant factors have been taken into consideration, susceptible to being deemed to be such as to merit a final verdict of having been by no means unsatisfactory in its overall outcome and, in the final analysis, to give grounds for being judged, on mature reflection, to have been conducive to generating a degree of gratification which will be seen in retrospect to have been significantly higher than the general average.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Are you trying to say "Happy Christmas," Humphrey?

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Yes, Minister.
The Home Secretary has been forced to resign after a drunk-driving incident

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: What will happen to him?

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Well, I gather he was as drunk as a lord. So, after a discreet interval, they'll probably make him one.
The EEC wants to standardise sausages, and it turns out British bangers are not up to the standard

lines.speaker: Hacker
