lines.text: By the end of next year, we shall be waving good-bye to the good old British sausage, and we'll be forced to accept some foreign muck like salami or bratwurst or something in its place.

lines.speaker: Bernard
lines.text: They can't stop us eating the British sausage, can they?

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: They can stop us calling it the sausage, though. Apparently, it's going to be called the "emulsified high-fat offal tube".

lines.speaker: Bernard
lines.text: And you swallowed it?
Bernard is waiting at the Hackers' flat for the Minister to come home

lines.speaker: Annie
lines.text: He's obviously been held up. You can stamp some of these cards for me while you're waiting if you like.

lines.speaker: Bernard
lines.text: Oh, but aren't they to constituents?

lines.speaker: Annie
lines.text: Yes.

lines.speaker: Bernard
lines.text: Well, that's not government business, Mrs Hacker, that's political activity. I'm not allowed to help with the Minister's political activities.

lines.speaker: Annie
lines.text: Suppose they were all to journalists?

lines.speaker: Bernard
lines.text: Oh, that would be alright.

lines.speaker: Annie
lines.text: They're all to journalists.

lines.speaker: Bernard
lines.text: Fine. I suppose licking is an essential part of relationships with the press.
Discussing possible reasons for the Prime Minister's early retirement

lines.speaker: Bernard
lines.text: Minister, I've heard something quite different.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: What?

lines.speaker: Bernard
lines.text: That there is £1 million worth of diamonds from South Africa in a Downing Street safe, but of course it's only a rumour.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Is that true?

lines.speaker: Bernard
lines.text: Oh, yes.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: So, there ARE all those diamonds in Downing Street!

lines.speaker: Bernard
lines.text: Are there?

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: You just said there were.

lines.speaker: Bernard
lines.text: No, I didn't.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Yes, you did! You said you'd heard this rumour, I said is it true, you said yes!

lines.speaker: Bernard
lines.text: I said yes, it was true that it was a rumour.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: You said you heard it was true!

lines.speaker: Bernard
lines.text: No, I said it was true that I heard it!

lines.speaker: Annie
lines.text: I'm sorry to cut into this important discussion, but do you believe it?

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: I believe I heard it. Oh, about the diamonds. No.

lines.speaker: Annie
lines.text: Is it impossible?

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: No, but it's never been officially denied. First rule in politics: never believe anything until it's officially denied.

lines.speaker: Sir Arnold
lines.text: So, will our next Prime Minister be our eminent Chancellor or our distinguished Foreign Secretary?

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: That's what I wanted to ask you, which do you think it should be?

lines.speaker: Sir Arnold
lines.text: Hmmm. Difficult, like asking which lunatic should run the asylum.

lines.speaker: Sir Arnold
lines.text: Have we any allies?

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Oh, quite a few yes; the Chief Whip, particularly. But he's worried that whichever gets the job will antagonise the other's supporters and split the party.

lines.speaker: Sir Arnold
lines.text: So we're looking for a compromise candidate.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Hmm. Malleable.

lines.speaker: Sir Arnold
lines.text: Flexible.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Likeable.

lines.speaker: Sir Arnold
lines.text: No firm opinions.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: No bright ideas.

lines.speaker: Sir Arnold
lines.text: Not intellectually committed.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Without the strength of purpose to change anything.

lines.speaker: Sir Arnold
lines.text: Someone who you know can be manipula— professionally guided.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: And leave the business of government in the hands of the experts.
Long beat as Sir Arnold and Sir Humphrey slowly realise Hacker is the perfect candidate. They catch each other's eye and burst into uproarious laughter.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Bernard, what would you say to your present master as the next Prime Minister?

lines.speaker: Bernard
lines.text: The Minister?

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Yes.

lines.speaker: Bernard
lines.text: Mr Hacker?

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Yes.

lines.speaker: Bernard
lines.text: As Prime Minister?

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Yes.
Bernard checks his watch

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Are you in a hurry?

lines.speaker: Bernard
lines.text: No; I'm just checking to see it wasn't April the First.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: [Talking about his promotion] The relationship which I might tentatively venture to aver has been not without some degree of reciprocal utility and perhaps even occasional gratification, is approaching a point of irreversible bifurcation and, to be brief, is in the propinquity of its ultimate regrettable termination.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: ... I see.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: I'm... on my way out.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: What?

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: There comes a time when one has to accept what fate has in store. When one passes on.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: [horrified] Passes on!?

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: To pastures new, perhaps greener, and places oneself finally in the service of one who is greater than any of us.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Humphrey... I'm so sorry.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Oh, thank you, Minister.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Does Lady Appleby know?

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Well, she's suspected it for some time, apparently.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: When did they tell you?

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: This afternoon.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: How long did they give you?

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Oh, just a few weeks...

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: [horrified] A few weeks!?

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Well, it'll give me enough time to sort everything out.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: [his eyes filling with tears] Oh Humphrey, you're so terribly brave.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Well, one is a little anxious of course. One is always rather wary of the unknown, but I have faith somehow I'll muddle through.
Hacker takes his handkerchief out of his pocket and begins to cry into it

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Minister, what is the matter?

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: I am sorry, Humphrey. Just, well we had our ups and downs.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Oh Minister, do not take on so. We will still be seeing one another regularly. Yes, once a week at least.
Hacker looks up, aghast

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: What??

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: I have not told you where I am going yet. I have been appointed Secretary to the Cabinet.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Secretary to the Cabinet?

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: What did you think I meant?

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: I thought, I..., I....

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: How are things at the Campaign for Freedom of Information?

lines.speaker: Sir Arnold
lines.text: I'm sorry, I can't talk about it.
Hacker, Humphrey and Chief Whip Jeffery are talking about Hacker's campaign on Prime Ministership

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: But supposing somebody would say "Does that mean you refuse to stand?" You know how these media people try to trap you.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Well, Minister, it's not my place, but on previous occasions, a generally acceptable answer has been "While one does not seek the office, one has pledged oneself to the service of one's country. And if one's friends were to persuade one that that was the best way one could serve, one might reluctantly have to accept the responsibility, whatever one's own private wishes might be."

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: [taking notes] "...private wishes might be." yes, I think I've got that.
Jim Hacker and Maurice, the EEC Commissioner, are having a meeting to discuss the EEC plans to name British sausages 'emulsified high fat offal tubes':

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: One of your officials pays farmers to produce surplus food, while on the same floor, the next office is paying them to destroy the surpluses.

lines.speaker: Maurice
lines.text: That is not true!

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: No?

lines.speaker: Maurice
lines.text: He is not in the next office, not even on the same floor!

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Open government, Prime Minister. Freedom of information. We should always tell the press freely and frankly anything that they could easily find out some other way.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Wouldn't anybody... argue with me?

lines.speaker: General Howard
lines.text: Serving officers obey orders without question!

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: What if I were to get drunk?

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: On the whole, it would be safer if you didn't.

lines.speaker: Bernard
lines.text: Prime Minister, isn't conscription a courageous policy?

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: [panicking a bit] Courageous? Oh my God, is it?

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: With Trident we could obliterate the whole of Eastern Europe.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: I don't want to obliterate the whole of Eastern Europe.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: But it's a deterrent.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: It's a bluff. I probably wouldn't use it.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Yes, but they don't know that you probably wouldn't.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: They probably do.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Yes, they probably know that you probably wouldn't. But they can't certainly know.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: They probably certainly know that I probably wouldn't.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Yes, but even though they probably certainly know that you probably wouldn't, they don't certainly know that although you probably wouldn't, there is no probability that you certainly would!

lines.speaker: General Howard
lines.text: We don't need it. Complete waste of money. Totally unnecessary.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Well, that's what I said!

lines.speaker: General Howard
lines.text: You're right.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: And the whole defence staff agree?

lines.speaker: General Howard
lines.text: No, the Navy want to keep it. It's launched from their submarines. Take away Trident, they'd hardly have a role left.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: And the RAF?

lines.speaker: General Howard
lines.text: Well, you could ask them if you're interested in the opinion of garage mechanics.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: If you walked into a nuclear missile showroom, you would buy Trident. It's lovely, it's elegant, it's beautiful – it's quite simply the best, and Britain should have the best. In the world of the nuclear missile, it is the Savile Row suit, the Rolls-Royce Corniche, the Château Lafite 1945. It is the nuclear missile Harrods would sell you. What more can I say?

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Only that it costs fifteen billion pounds and we don't need it.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Well, you could say that about anything at Harrods!

lines.speaker: Bernard
lines.text: But he's the Prime Minister!

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Indeed he is, Bernard. He has his own car, a nice house in London, a place in the country, endless publicity and a pension for life. What more does he want?

lines.speaker: Bernard
lines.text: I think he wants to govern Britain.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Well, stop him, Bernard.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Bernard, what is the purpose of our defence policy?

lines.speaker: Bernard
lines.text: To defend Britain.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: No, Bernard. It is to make people believe Britain is defended.

lines.speaker: Bernard
lines.text: The Russians?

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Not the Russians, the British! The Russians know it's not.

lines.speaker: Godfrey
lines.text: Will you be wearing those glasses?

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Oh, well, what do you think?

lines.speaker: Godfrey
lines.text: Well, it's up to you, obviously. With them on, you look authoritative and commanding; with them off, you look honest and open. Which do you want?

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Well, really, I want to look authoritative and honest.

lines.speaker: Godfrey
lines.text: It's one or the other, really.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: What about starting with them off, and then just putting them on when I talk?

lines.speaker: Godfrey
lines.text: That just looks indecisive.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: I see.

lines.speaker: Bernard
lines.text: What about a monocle?

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: [reading a speech written for him] "We shall of course be reviewing a wide range of options over the whole field of government expenditures." Bernard, this doesn't say anything.

lines.speaker: Bernard
lines.text: Oh, thank you, Prime Minister.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: It's completely lacking impact.

lines.speaker: Bernard
lines.text: You're too kind, Prime Minster.

lines.speaker: Permanent Secretary for Health
lines.text: It would be different if the Government were a team, but in fact they're a loose confederation of warring tribes.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: The statistics are irrefutable...

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Statistics? You can prove anything with statistics.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Even the truth.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Yes... No!

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Notwithstanding the fact that your proposal could conceivably encompass certain concomitant benefits of a marginal and peripheral relevance, there is a countervailing consideration of infinitely superior magnitude involving your personal complicity and corroborative malfeasance, with a consequence that the taint and stigma of your former associations and diversions could irredeemably and irretrievably invalidate your position and culminate in public revelations and recriminations of a profoundly embarrassing and ultimately indefensible character.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Perhaps I can have a précis of that?

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: He’s got to learn to come to heel. He’s got to learn to 'co-operate'.

lines.speaker: Bernard
lines.text: What do you mean 'co-operate'?

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: I mean obey my commands! That's what 'co-operate' means when you're Prime Minister.

lines.speaker: Bernard
lines.text: Sir Humphrey's waiting to see you outside.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Send him in, at once!

lines.speaker: Bernard
lines.text: Yes, Prime Minister. Your word is my 'co-operation'.
Sir Humphrey is not happy that Hacker has decided to move Dorothy Wainwright back into her old office, which was turned into a waiting room on Sir Humphrey's orders while she was away on holiday.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: People can wait in the lobby or in the state rooms.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Some people, but some people must wait where other people cannot see the people who are waiting; and people who arrive before other people must wait where they cannot see the people who arrive after them being admitted before them; and people who come in from outside must wait where they cannot see the people from inside coming in to tell you what the people from outside have come to see you about; and people who arrive when you are with people they are not supposed to know you have seen must wait somewhere until the people who are not supposed to have seen you have seen you.
Jim is trying to explain to Dorothy why he's changed his mind about moving her back to her old office

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: ...That is, if people saw people coming, before people saw them seeing people, people would see people! The whole ship would go off the rails - you see?

lines.speaker: Dorothy
lines.text: Did you work all that out for yourself?
Sir Humphrey is not happy that Bernard has deprived him of his key to Number 10

lines.speaker: Bernard
lines.text: Well, I believe it's the Prime Minister's decision who comes into his house. After all, I don't give my mother-in-law the key to my house.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: [furiously] I am not the Prime Minister's mother-in-law, Bernard!

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: But me no buts, Bernard. Shakespeare.

lines.speaker: Bernard
lines.text: Oh no, Prime Minister. "But me no buts" is circa 1820. Mrs. Centlivre used the phrase in 1708, but actually it was Scott's employment of it in The Antiquary in 1816 which made it fashionable.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Shall we keep to the point please, Bernard?

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: I wanted to sound you out about something.

lines.speaker: Sir Frank Gordon
lines.text: Of course, Prime Minister.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: It's about Humphrey. I wonder if he hasn't got rather too much on his plate.

lines.speaker: Sir Frank Gordon
lines.text: Oh I'm sure he can manage. Tremendously able.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: You don't think he is overstretched?

lines.speaker: Sir Frank Gordon
lines.text: Oh no, got it all under control. No problem there.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: I see, because I was wondering, speculating of course, about his position as the head of the civil service.

lines.speaker: Sir Frank Gordon
lines.text: Ah...

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: It could make some sense if everything were to be transferred to the Treasury if you think you could do part of Humphrey's job.

lines.speaker: Sir Frank Gordon
lines.text: Oh... Yes, that could make a lot of sense.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: But if as you say he's not overstretched...

lines.speaker: Sir Frank Gordon
lines.text: Ah, when I say not 'overstretched', I was of course talking in the sense of total cumulative loading taken globally, rather than in respect of certain individual and essentially anomalous responsibilities which are not, logically speaking, consonant or harmonious with the broad spectrum of intermeshing and inseparable functions and could indeed be said to place an excessive and supererogatory burden on the office when considered in relation to the comparatively exiguous advantages of their overall centralization.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: You could do part of Humphrey's job!

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Prime Minister, I must protest in the strongest possible terms my profound opposition to the newly instituted practice which imposes severe and intolerable restrictions upon the ingress and egress of senior members of the hierarchy and will, in all probability, should the current deplorable innovation be perpetuated, precipitate a constriction of the channels of communication, and culminate in a condition of organisational atrophy and administrative paralysis, which will render effectively impossible the coherent and co-ordinated discharge of the function of government within Her Majesty's United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland!

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: You mean you've lost your key?
The PM is considering taking the joint headship of the civil service away from Humphrey and making Frank the full head

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Oh, Frank.

lines.speaker: Sir Frank Gordon
lines.text: Yes?

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Good meeting with the PM?

lines.speaker: Sir Frank Gordon
lines.text: Yes, very good.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Good. Any particular subject come up?

lines.speaker: Sir Frank Gordon
lines.text: Any particular subject you're interested in?

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: No, not particularly. He didn't raise the issue of service appointments and so on?

lines.speaker: Sir Frank Gordon
lines.text: It may have cropped up.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Did he foreshadow any redistribution of responsibility?

lines.speaker: Sir Frank Gordon
lines.text: Shall we say it was a wide-ranging discussion.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Did it move towards any conclusion?

lines.speaker: Sir Frank Gordon
lines.text: There were arguments on both sides.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Evenly balanced?

lines.speaker: Sir Frank Gordon
lines.text: Perhaps tending slightly more one way than the other.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: But nothing to worry about?

lines.speaker: Sir Frank Gordon
lines.text: Nothing for me to worry about. See you this afternoon.
Hacker has just had a stormy cabinet meeting over a sudden financial crisis.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Bernard, Humphrey should have seen this coming and warned me.

lines.speaker: Bernard
lines.text: I don't think Sir Humphrey understands economics, Prime Minister; he did read Classics, you know.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: What about Sir Frank? He's head of the Treasury!

lines.speaker: Bernard
lines.text: Well I'm afraid he's at an even greater disadvantage in understanding economics: he's an economist.
Hacker complains about the MP deputation came to him to ask for a pay rise.

lines.speaker: Annie
lines.text: But aren't they underpaid in fact?

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Underpaid? Backbench MPs, Darling, being an MP is a vast subsidised ego trip. It's a job for which you need no qualifications, no compulsory hours of work, no performance standards. A warm room and subsidised meals for a bunch of self-opinionated windbags and busybodies who suddenly find people taking them seriously because they got letters "MP" after their names. How can they be underpaid when there're about two hundred applicants for every vacancy? You could fill every seat twenty times over even if they have to pay to do the job.
Hacker asks Humphrey about the sudden financial crisis.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Why the sudden crisis? The Treasury must've seen it coming.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Prime Minister, I'm not the Permanent Secretary to the Treasury. You must ask Sir Frank.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: What would Sir Frank say?

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: It is not for a humble mortal such as I to speculate on the complex and elevated deliberations of the mighty. But in general, I think Sir Frank believes that if the Treasury knows something has to be done, the Cabinet shouldn't have too much time to think about it.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: But that's an outrageous view!

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Yes, indeed. It's known as Treasury policy.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Suppose the Cabinet has questions?

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Well I think Sir Frank's view is that on the rare occasions when the Treasury understands the questions, the Cabinet doesn't understand the answers.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Real reductions in the size of the Service?! It'd be the end of civilisation as we know it!
Bernard is trying to tell Sir Humphrey about a confidential conversation.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: You're speaking in riddles, Bernard.

lines.speaker: Bernard
lines.text: Oh, thank you, Sir Humphrey.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: That was not a compliment, Bernard!
Hacker is discussing Humphrey's two responsibilities.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: It's so difficult for me, you see, as I'm wearing two hats.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Yes, isn't that rather awkward for you?

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Not if one is in two minds.

lines.speaker: Bernard
lines.text: Or has two faces.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: If there were a conflict of interests which side would the civil service really be on?

lines.speaker: Bernard
lines.text: The winning side, Prime Minister.

episodes.title: A Victory for Democracy
episodes.titleFull: Episode Six: A Victory for Democracy

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: I gather we're planning to vote against Israel in the UN tonight.

lines.speaker: Foreign Secretary
lines.text: Of course.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Why?

lines.speaker: Foreign Secretary
lines.text: They bombed the PLO.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: But the PLO bombed Israel!

lines.speaker: Foreign Secretary
lines.text: Yes, but the Israelis dropped more bombs than the PLO did.
Bernard pulls the Prime Minister away from Luke for a private conversation.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: You just said that the Foreign Office was keeping something from me! How do you know if you don't know?

lines.speaker: Bernard
lines.text: I don't know specifically what, Prime Minister, but I do know that the Foreign Office always keep everything from everybody. It's normal practice.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Who does know?

lines.speaker: Bernard
lines.text: May I just clarify the question? You are asking who would know what it is that I don't know and you don't know but the Foreign Office know that they know that they are keeping from you so that you don't know but they do know and all we know there is something we don't know and we want to know but we don't know what because we don't know! Is that it?

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: May I clarify the question: Who knows Foreign Office secrets, apart from the Foreign Office?

lines.speaker: Bernard
lines.text: Oh, that's easy: only the Kremlin.
Hacker has just requested a goodwill visit to St George's Island.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: He [the defence secretary] seemed to think 800 fully armed paratroopers was an awful lot to send on a goodwill visit.

lines.speaker: Israeli Ambassador
lines.text: No, it is just an awful lot of goodwill!

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Oh, this is nice. The Americans are delighted by our little visit to St. George's Island. That's good, isn't it?

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: [resigned] Excellent.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: They say they have got a whole airborne division ready if we want reinforcements.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: [sharply] Reinforcements of what?

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Reinforcements of goodwill, Humphrey!

lines.speaker: Bernard
lines.text: What if the Prime Minister insists we help them?

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Then we follow the four-stage strategy.

lines.speaker: Bernard
lines.text: What's that?

lines.speaker: Sir Richard Wharton
lines.text: Standard Foreign Office response in a time of crisis.

lines.speaker: Sir Richard Wharton
lines.text: In stage one we say nothing is going to happen.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Stage two, we say something may be about to happen, but we should do nothing about it.

lines.speaker: Sir Richard Wharton
lines.text: In stage three, we say that maybe we should do something about it, but there's nothing we *can* do.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Stage four, we say maybe there was something we could have done, but it's too late now.

lines.speaker: Bernard
lines.text: What if he demands options?

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Well, it's obvious, Bernard. The Foreign Office will happily present him with three options, two of which are, on close inspection, exactly the same.

lines.speaker: Sir Richard Wharton
lines.text: Plus a third which is totally unacceptable.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Like bombing Warsaw or invading France.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Bishops tend to have long lives. Apparently the Lord isn't all that keen to let them join him.

lines.speaker: Man
lines.text: In such an awful country, they cut people's hands off and women get stoned when they commit adultery.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Unlike Britain, where they commit adultery when they get stoned.

lines.speaker: Peter Harding
lines.text: Soames has been waiting for a bishopric for years.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Long time, no see.

lines.speaker: Bernard
lines.text: It's one of those irregular verbs, isn't it: I have an independent mind; you are an eccentric; he is round the twist.
See also w:emotive conjugation for Bertrand Russell's original 1948 version.
Sir Humphrey is suspected of having once been a Russian spy.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: So what do you think I should do, Arnold?

lines.speaker: Sir Arnold
lines.text: [calmly pours his coffee] Hmm, difficult. Depends a bit on whether you actually were spying or not. [notices Sir Humphrey's horrified expression] One must keep an open mind.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: But I couldn't have been! I wasn't at Cambridge!

lines.speaker: Sir Arnold
lines.text: If once they accepted the principle that senior Civil Servants could be removed for incompetence, that would be the thin end of the wedge. We could lose dozens of our chaps. Hundreds, perhaps.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Thousands.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: It is characteristic of all committee discussions and decisions that every member has a vivid recollection of them and that every member’s recollection of them differs violently from every other member’s recollection. Consequently, we accept the convention that the official decisions are those and only those which have been officially recorded in the minutes by the officials, from which it emerges with an elegant inevitability that any decision which has been officially reached will have been officially recorded in the minutes by the officials and any decision which is not recorded in the minutes has not been officially reached even if one or more members believe they can recollect it, so in this particular case, if the decision had been officially reached it would have been officially recorded in the minutes by the officials, and it isn’t, so it wasn’t.

lines.speaker: Bernard
lines.text: That's another of those irregular verbs, isn't it? I give confidential press briefings; you leak; he's being charged under section 2A of the Official Secrets Act.
Lunch with a newspaper editor

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: So I want you to retract that suppression story.

lines.speaker: Burnham
lines.text: I don't see how I can.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Well, of course you can! You're the editor, aren't you?

lines.speaker: Burnham
lines.text: Yes, but an editor isn't like a general commanding an army; he's just the ringmaster of a circus. I mean I can book the acts, but I can't tell the acrobats which way to jump!

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Gratitude is merely a lively expectation of favours to come. Reference to François de La Rochefoucauld

lines.speaker: Bernard
lines.text: The problem is, the prime minister *did* try to suppress the chapter, didn't he.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: I don't know, did he?

lines.speaker: Bernard
lines.text: Well, didn't he? Don't you remember?

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: What I remember is irrelevant, Bernard. If the minutes don't say that he did, then he didn't.

lines.speaker: Bernard
lines.text: So you want me to falsify the minutes?

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: I want nothing of the sort! It's up to you, Bernard - what do you want?

lines.speaker: Bernard
lines.text: I want to have a clear conscience.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: A clear conscience.

lines.speaker: Bernard
lines.text: Yes!

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: When did you acquire this taste for luxuries? Consciences are for politicians, Bernard! We are humble functionaries whose duty it is to implement the commands of our democratically elected representatives. How could we possibly be doing anything wrong if it has been commanded by those who represent the people?

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: You choose from a jumble of ill-digested ideas a version which represents the Prime Minister's views as he would, on reflection, have liked them to emerge.

lines.speaker: Bernard
lines.text: But if it's not a true record...

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: The purpose of minutes is not to record events, it is to protect people. You do not take notes if the Prime Minister says something he did not mean to say, particularly if it contradicts something he has said publicly.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Don't we ever get our own way with the French?

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Well, sometimes.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: When was the last time?

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Battle of Waterloo, 1815.

lines.speaker: Bernard
lines.text: [on the phone] Yes, we will want simultaneous translators. No, not when the PM meets the leaders of the English-speaking nations. Yes, the English-speaking nations can be said to include the United States. With a certain generosity of spirit.

lines.speaker: Bernard
lines.text: [on the phone] No we can't have alphabetical sitting in the Abbey, you would have Iran and Iraq sitting together, plus Jordan and Israel all in the same pew, we would be in danger of starting World War Three. No! I know Ireland begins with an I but No! Ireland doesn’t make it any better, Ireland doesn’t make anything any better.

episodes.title: A Conflict of Interest
episodes.titleFull: Episode Four: A Conflict of Interest

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: The only way to understand the Press is to remember that they pander to their readers' prejudices.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Don't tell me about the press. I know exactly who reads the papers: The Daily Mirror is read by people who think they run the country; The Guardian is read by people who think they ought to run the country; The Times is read by the people who actually do run the country; The Daily Mail is read by the wives of the people who run the country; The Financial Times is read by people who own the country; The Morning Star is read by people who think the country ought to be run by another country; and The Daily Telegraph is read by people who think it is.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Oh and Prime Minister, what about the people who read The Sun?

lines.speaker: Bernard
lines.text: Sun readers don't care who runs the country as long as she's got big tits.

episodes.title: Power to the People
episodes.titleFull: Episode Five: Power to the People

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Bernard, if the right people don’t have power, do you know what happens? The wrong people get it: politicians, councillors, ordinary voters!

lines.speaker: Bernard
lines.text: But aren’t they supposed to, in a democracy?

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: This is a British democracy, Bernard!

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: To put it simply, Prime Minister, certain informal discussions took place involving a full and frank exchange of views out of which there arose a series of proposals, which on examination proved to indicate certain promising lines of inquiry, which, when pursued, lead to the realization that the alternative courses of action might, in fact, in certain circumstances, be susceptible of discreet modification, leading to a reappraisal of the original areas of difference and pointing the way to encouraging possibilities of compromise and cooperation, which, if bilaterally implemented with appropriate give and take on both sides might, if the climate were right, have a reasonable probability at the end of the day of leading, rightly or wrongly, to a mutually satisfactory resolution.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: What the hell are you talking about?

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: We did a deal.

lines.speaker: Sir Arnold
lines.text: It's the old logical fallacy: "all cats have fours legs, my dog has four legs...

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: ...therefore my dog is a cat."

lines.speaker: Sir Arnold
lines.text: He's suffering from politician's logic.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: "Something must be done, this is something, therefore we must do it."

lines.speaker: Sir Arnold
lines.text: But doing the wrong thing is worse than doing nothing.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Doing anything is worse than doing nothing.

episodes.title: The Patron of the Arts
episodes.titleFull: Episode Six: The Patron of the Arts

lines.speaker: Bernard
lines.text: If there was a major crisis, you wouldn't need to go at all.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Is there a major crisis coming up?

lines.speaker: Bill
lines.text: Not really, Prime Minister.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Is there a distant crisis, that we could bring forward?

lines.speaker: Bernard
lines.text: I know, what about the death of a cabinet colleague?

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Ooh, is one imminent?

lines.speaker: Bill
lines.text: Well we can hardly hope for that to fall on the right day. Well, not by accident.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Sir Humphrey, I need help.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: You do. You do?

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: I've got to make a speech. It could be very embarrassing.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Oh Prime Minister, your speeches are nothing like as embarrassing as they used to be!

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: I didn't say the speech would be embarrassing, Sir Humphrey. I said the occasion could be.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Ah, yes, yes, indeed. Why?

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: It's to be to a hostile audience of posturing, self-righteous, theatrical drunks.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: The House of Commons, you mean?

lines.speaker: Bill
lines.text: There's a lot of terrible publicity if you take [arts money] away. The arts lobby is part of the educated middle class. It's one of the few ways they can get their income tax back. Mortgage tax relief, university grants, lump-sum pensions, Radio 3, and cheap subsidised seats at the theatre, opera and the concerts. You can't begrudge it us... them!

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: They do some good.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: They don't, Prime Minister! They hardly do anything at all.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Well let's abolish them!

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: No, no, no, no!

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Well of course we'll do what we can, but there are many calls on the public purse, you know. Inner cities, schools, hospitals, kidney machines...

lines.speaker: Ladies
lines.text: Tanks, rockets, H-bombs.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Well we can't really defend ourselves against the Russians with a performance of "Henry V".

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Dorothy, you've got to help me. This is a real hot potato. If I don't do anything, it could turn into a banana skin.

lines.speaker: Bernard
lines.text: Prime Minister, a hot potato can't become a banana skin.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: What?

lines.speaker: Bernard
lines.text: Well if you don't do anything, a hot potato just becomes a cold potato.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Nobody would be able to call me a philistine then!

lines.speaker: Dorothy
lines.text: Not unless they knew you.

episodes.title: The National Education Service
episodes.titleFull: Episode Seven: The National Education Service

lines.speaker: Bernard
lines.text: Sir Humphrey, he's very worried that he seems responsible for something that he can't change.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Yes, I'm sure. Responsibility without power: the prerogative of the eunuch throughout the ages.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: I think education is extremely important. It could lose me the next election.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Ah! In my naivety, I thought you were concerned about the future of our children.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Yes, that too. After all, they get the vote at 18.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: [reading from a list of quiz questions] Maths has become politicized - "If it costs 5 billion pounds a year to maintain Britain's nuclear defenses, and 75 pounds a year to feed a starving African child, how many African children could be saved from starvation if the Ministry of Defense abandoned nuclear weapons?"

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: That's easy, none. They'd spend it all on conventional weapons.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Education in this country is a disaster. We're supposed to be preparing children for a working life. Three-quarters of the time, they're bored stiff!

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Well, I should have thought that being bored stiff for three-quarters of the time was an excellent preparation for working life.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: The school leaving age was raised to 16 so they could learn more, and they're learning less.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: We didn't raise it to enable them to learn more, we raised it to keep teenagers off the job market and hold down the unemployment figures.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Are you saying there's nothing wrong with education in this country?

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: No, of course not Prime Minister, it's a joke! It's always been a joke! And as long as your leave it in the hands of the local councillors, it will remain a joke. I mean, half of them are your enemies anyway, and the other half are the sort of friends who make you prefer your enemies.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Well, what are you saying?

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: I'm saying that education will never get any better as long as it's subject to all that tomfoolery in the town halls. I mean, just imagine what would happen if you put defense in the hands of the local authorities.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Defense?

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Yes, give the local councils 100 million each and ask them to defend themselves. We wouldn't have to worry about the Russians, we'd have a civil war in three weeks!

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Better than Channel 4 coverage. They didn't describe it as the PM's tour of the north-west. They said, "Jim Hacker touring the marginal constituencies."

lines.speaker: Annie
lines.text: That's true, isn't it?

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: But they shouldn't say it. It's biased reporting!

lines.speaker: Annie
lines.text: Reporting the facts?

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Nothing wrong with visiting the marginals.

lines.speaker: Annie
lines.text: What they said was still true.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: It was still biased to say it!
The Prime Minister believes that he gave a clear, simple, straightforward and honest answer.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Unfortunately, although the answer was indeed clear, simple, and straightforward, there is some difficulty in justifiably assigning to it the fourth of the epithets you applied to the statement, inasmuch as the precise correlation between the information you communicated and the facts, insofar as they can be determined and demonstrated, is such as to cause epistemological problems, of sufficient magnitude as to lay upon the logical and semantic resources of the English language a heavier burden than they can reasonably be expected to bear.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Epistemological — what are you talking about?

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: You told a lie.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: A lie?

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: A lie.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: What do you mean, a lie?

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: I mean you… lied. Yes, I know this is a difficult concept to get across to a politician. You… ah yes, you did not tell the truth.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: You mean we are bugging Hugh Halifax's telephones?

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: We were.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: We were? When did we stop?

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: [checks his watch] Seventeen minutes ago.

lines.speaker: Bernard
lines.text: The fact that you needed to know was not known at the time that the now known need to know was known, and therefore those that needed to advise and inform the Home Secretary perhaps felt that the information that he needed as to whether to inform the highest authority of the known information was not yet known, and therefore there was no authority for the authority to be informed because the need to know was not, at that time, known or needed.
Final lines. Sir Humphrey enters the Cabinet Room

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Ah, Humphrey, come in, come in, come in! (Chuckles) How did your broadcast go?

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Oh, very well, very well.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: What did you say?

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Oh, nothing in particular. I think I pointed out some of the difficulties in allocating responsibilities as between politicians and civil servants.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: But you were discreet?

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Why do you ask?

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Were you or weren't you?

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Yes.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Yes, you were or yes, you weren't?

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Yes.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Humpy?

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Wouldn't you expect me to be discreet?

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Yes, of course.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: There you are, then.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Good. Well, that's all right, then, isn't it?

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Why do you ask, Prime Minister?

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Well, it's just that the BBC sent me a tape.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: A tape? What tape?

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: A tape of your broadcast. I thought we might listen to it together.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Oh, no, no, no, no, no, no, no, no.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Why not?

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: No, it isn't at all interesting.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Not interesting? The Cabinet Secretary talking to the nation?

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Well, not VERY interesting.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: You mean you were too discreet? (to Bernard) Play it, would you, Bernard?
Bernard plays the tape

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: [on tape. We hear what Humphrey said after he assumed recording had stopped.] My dear Ludo, nobody tells the truth about unemployment.

lines.speaker: Ludovic Kennedy
lines.text: [on tape] Oh, why not?

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: [on tape] Because everyone knows you can halve it in a few weeks.

lines.speaker: Ludovic Kennedy
lines.text: [on tape] How?

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: [on tape] Cut off all Social Security to all claimants who refuse two job offers. There's genuine unemployment in the north...

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Humphrey!

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: I'm terribly sorry, Prime Minister, I didn't know! They didn't tell me! The interview was over!

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: The indiscretion! The irresponsibility! Is there any more?

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: No.

lines.speaker: Bernard
lines.text: Yes.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Play it, Bernard.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: : [on tape] ...may be off the register as soon as you could say "parasite". Frankly, this country can have as much unemployment as it's prepared to pay for in social security, and no politicians have got the guts to do anything about it!
Bernard stops the tape.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: You said that!?

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: It was Mike Yarwood...

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: I'm in somewhat of a difficulty as to know what to do about this, Humphrey. I think I need advice.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Advice?

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Perhaps I ought to play it to the Cabinet, get their reaction.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Oh, please!

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Or the Privy Council.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Oh, please!

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Or... Her Majesty?

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Oh, God!

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Do you realise what this would mean if it got into the papers, the damage it would do to me, to the government?

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: I could say I got it wrong! I've checked, it isn't true!

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: But it is true.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: But I could say it isn't! Nobody can prove it, it's never been tried!

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: You would tell an untruth in public?

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Yes, for YOU, Prime Minister! We can issue a clarification.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: I think you already made yourself very clear.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: No, Prime Minister, a clarification is not to make oneself clear, it is to put oneself IN the clear.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: "Oh, what a tangled web we weave". (to Bernard) Give me the tape, would you, Bernard? (Bernard gives him the tape and Hacker turns back to Sir Humphrey) Now I've got something to tell you. (Shows Sir Humphrey the tape) This is a copy... (Takes out the film reel from inside his jacket) ...but this is the original, the master.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: You mean?

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: They were retrieved from the BBC.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: By whom?

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Intelligence.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: So no one else will ever know?

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Well, that rather depends on what I choose to tell them. Of course, I could just hand over the tapes or... I could hold onto them while I consider the security and disciplinary implications. I certainly have no intention of joining "some shabby cover-up". Oh, that reminds me, have you decided yet what you're going to tell the Privileges Committee?

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Oh, yes, yes, Prime Minister. I've decided that, uh, in the interests of national security, that, um, the only honourable course is to support your statement in the House.

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: And say that Hugh Halifax's telephone has never been bugged?

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: And say I have no evidence?

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: No, Humphrey, and say the government has never authorised the bugging of MPs' telephones.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: ...say the government has never author... Supposing they find out the truth?

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: You'll just have to say that nobody told you, because you didn't need to know. Agreed? (Sir Humphrey sighs) Splendid. Well, that's settled, then.

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: May one have one's tapes back?
Hacker extends the cassette and the original tape reel toward Humphrey but then withdraws them

lines.speaker: Hacker
lines.text: Tomorrow. After the Committee on Privileges. All right, Humphrey?

lines.speaker: Sir Humphrey
lines.text: Yes, Prime Minister. (Leaves the table)
